mappings.name: basicuserinfo: the documented body, for a number the rail knows

why: MTN's DOCUMENTED 200 for GetBasicUserinfo, transcribed field for field from the
operation's own OpenAPI components on the MoMo developer portal, retrieved
2026-09-05 (the citation, with the exact URL, is in
docs/plans/issue-47-notes/impl.md and docs/flows/account-holder-lookup.md).
Six fields: given_name, family_name, birthdate, locale, gender, status.
FOUR OF THE SIX ARE HERE PRECISELY SO THEY CAN BE PROVEN TO DIE.
vpay_adapter_mtn_momo::wire::BasicUserInfo deserialises the two name fields and
has no home for the rest, so serde drops them at the first point the bytes
become a Rust value. A stub that sent only the two names would make
`an_account_holder_lookup_returns_a_name_and_nothing_else` pass whether or not
the projection existed -- which is the shape of a test that proves nothing.
THE PATH IS LOWER-CASE `msisdn`, and MTN's own portal declares the
accountHolderIdType enum UPPER-case (MSISDN | Email | Alias | ID) while every
published example spells the segment lower-case. This mapping pins EXACTLY what
the adapter sends (vpay_adapter_mtn_momo::ACCOUNT_HOLDER_ID_TYPE), so a change
of case is a 404 here rather than a silent difference against the real sandbox --
which vpay has never called. See docs/flows/account-holder-lookup.md, 'unverified
against the real rail'.
237600000200 is in the same 2376000000xx documentation block every other MSISDN
in this directory comes from, and is DIGITS ONLY: `/v1/account_holders` validates
Cameroon E.164 server-side, so a hex-lettered steering number of the kind
requesttopay.json uses could not reach this endpoint from the API at all.

mappings.name: basicuserinfo: a number the rail has no record of

why: The row the whole port method exists for: 404 -> Ok(None), 'the rail has no
record', which a caller may act on as a fact about the NUMBER. Everything else
that is not a 200 is an Err, because reporting a lookup that did not happen as
Ok(None) would tell the caller a real account is unregistered.
AN ASSUMPTION, STATED. MTN documents NO 404 for GetBasicUserinfo -- the portal
lists 200, 401 and 500 for it, where RequesttoPayTransactionStatus documents
'404 Resource not found' explicitly. This mapping and the adapter's arm are
therefore a deliberate assumption rather than a transcription: a 404 is the only
status a REST resource has for 'no such thing', and the assumption is safe in the
direction that matters -- if MTN never sends one the arm is dead code, and if it
sends one for another reason the caller's fail-closed rule still refuses. The
body is spelled the way MTN's other not-found bodies are; nothing reads it.
`a_number_the_rail_has_no_record_of_is_not_an_error` is what this serves.

mappings.name: basicuserinfo: answered, but far too slowly

why: Two orders of magnitude above the suite's SHORT_REQUEST_TIMEOUT (100 ms), so the
assertion is about ProviderConfig::request_timeout firing and not about a slow CI
machine -- the same shape requesttopay-status.json's ...0560 mapping has, and the
same suffix, so the two read together.
A TIMEOUT AND NOT A 503, deliberately: a 503 produces a ProviderError::Transport
with no `source` (the rail answered, badly), whereas a deadline that fires
produces one carrying the reqwest error, which is what
`a_lookup_that_cannot_reach_the_rail_is_a_transport_error_never_a_missing_holder`
walks with vpay_core::error::source_chain. Reporting an unreachable rail as
Ok(None) is the single worst thing this method could do, and a source chain an
operator can read is how the real failure survives to a log.
The body is a VALID, NAMED holder on purpose: if the deadline were not applied
the adapter would parse it and answer Ok(Some(..)), so the case cannot pass for
the wrong reason.

mappings.name: basicuserinfo: a body far larger than any answer this rail documents

why: 300 KB, comfortably past vpay_provider::http::MAX_RAIL_BODY_BYTES (256 KiB) --
the same shape requesttopay-status.json's ...0b16 mapping has, for the same
reason: Response::text()/bytes() read to end of stream, so without the bound the
peer chooses how much memory a request handler allocates. This endpoint is
reachable from a MERCHANT-facing GET, so the peer would be choosing it once per
inbound request rather than once per charge.
The body is a valid, NAMED holder on purpose: if the bound were removed the
adapter would parse it and answer Ok(Some(..)), so the case cannot pass for the
wrong reason. Padded via --global-response-templating rather than a 300 KB
fixture file, which is not a thing to check into a repository.

mappings.name: basicuserinfo: a body carrying far more personal data than a name

why: THE PRIVACY CASE. Issue #47 section 3: this route returns a real person's name,
and MTN's body carries more than a name. The five fields below the documented six
-- sub, email, address, national_id, phone_number -- are NOT in MTN's published
schema; they are here on purpose, because the projection must survive a rail that
starts sending a field nobody planned for. serde drops an unknown field by
default, so a struct that models two fields drops eleven-minus-two whether or not
anyone remembered them.
`an_account_holder_body_of_personal_data_yields_a_name_and_leaks_nothing` asserts
both halves: that the returned value carries the NAME and none of the rest, and
that none of the rest -- nor the name, nor the number -- appears in the tracing
output captured around the call. The second half is the one a code change can
silently break: a `tracing::debug!(?body)` added to the adapter for debugging
would put every one of these strings in an operator's log, and nothing else in
this repository would notice.
A DIFFERENT NAME from the 237600000200 mapping's David Mbarga, so a test that
searched for the wrong holder's name cannot pass by accident.

mappings.name: basicuserinfo: demo — a number registered to a named holder

why: THE DEMO PAIR, keyed by MSISDN so `just demo` can show both answers of
GET /v1/account_holders against a stack it has already brought up.
237600000100 is the digits-only settling number the demo and
`a_digits_only_msisdn_reaches_the_same_walk_as_its_hex_twin` already use for a
payment that succeeds (see demo-outcomes.json), so the walkthrough can show one
number that both pays and has a name -- which is what a merchant's
nominated-destination check actually looks at. It steers nothing here: this is a
different URL space from /collection/v1_0/requesttopay, matched by exact path, so
it cannot interact with any scenario in this directory.
Priority 4 rather than 1 only to sit alongside the other demo mappings; nothing
competes for this path.
Its not-found twin is the next mapping. The two together are what let the demo
print 'verified: true, name: ...' and 'verified: false, name: null' from the same
route -- the distinction issue #47 exists to preserve.

mappings.name: basicuserinfo: demo — a number the rail has never seen

why: The demo's not-found half. 237600000199 steers nothing else in this directory --
it is not one of the 100/101/102 outcome numbers and not one of the hex family --
so it exists only to be a number with no holder.
It answers 404, which the adapter maps to Ok(None) and the route renders as
`{ name: null, verified: false }` with HTTP 200. A demo that showed the same
output for 'no such holder' and 'we could not ask' would be demonstrating the
opposite of what this route is for; see this file's not-found mapping above for
why the 404 itself is an assumption rather than a transcription.
